## Objectives {.unnumbered}

This lab accompanies the Week 4 notes, [*Data Wrangling I - Loading, Cleaning and Tidying*](https://soton-fds.github.io/week04.html).

- Load delimited data files into `R` using `readr`, and check that the data has loaded correctly.
- Use `dplyr` to filter, select, mutate, arrange, group and summarise data.
- Recognise whether a dataset is tidy, and use `tidyr` to tidy it by pivoting and separating columns.
- Chain operations together into readable pipelines using `|>`.

### Task 1: Loading Data

- [ ] The directory `data/part1/` contains three data files. Load them into `R` using `tidyverse`. (Hint: the three files are not all formatted in the same way.)
- [ ] By default, each `read_*` function prints a message describing the columns it has read. Make sure these messages are hidden.
- [ ] For each of the files, display the first few rows of the file.

::: {.solution}

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
read_csv("data/part1/data1.csv") |> head()
read_tsv("data/part1/data2.txt") |> head()
read_delim("data/part1/data3", delim = ";") |> head()
```

The chunk option `#| message: false` (see the Week 3 notes) only takes effect when the document is rendered; if you run the code in the console the messages will still appear.
As an aside, you can also hide the column messages for an individual `read_*` call by passing `show_col_types = FALSE`, which works wherever the code is run:

```{r}
read_csv("data/part1/data1.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |> head()
```

:::

### Task 1b: Checking Loaded Data

Getting data to load without an error is only the first step: `R` will happily load data in a way that is *wrong*.
You should always check that what you have loaded makes sense.
In this task we will look more closely at the three files from Task 1.

The file `data3` contains information about books in a bookshop.

- [ ] Look at the type of each column. Is the `ISBN` column stored sensibly? (Hint: an ISBN is an identifier; would it make sense to add two ISBNs together? What would happen to an ISBN that starts with a `0`?)
- [ ] Reload the file so that `ISBN` is stored as text. (Hint: look up the `col_types` argument of `read_delim`, and the `cols` and `col_character` functions.)
- [ ] `readr` also has a function called `read_csv2`, which reads files that use `;` as a delimiter. Try loading `data3` with `read_csv2` instead. Compare the `PriceUSD` and `AvgRating` columns to the raw file. What has gone wrong?

::: {.solution}

```{r}
books <- read_delim(
    "data/part1/data3",
    delim = ";",
    col_types = cols(ISBN = col_character()),
    show_col_types = FALSE
)
books |> select(Title, ISBN)
```

`ISBN` was originally read as a number (`<dbl>`), because it consists only of digits.
However it is an identifier, not a quantity: arithmetic on it is meaningless, and any leading zeros would be lost.
It should be stored as text.

```{r}
read_csv2("data/part1/data3", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
    select(Title, PriceUSD, AvgRating) |>
    head()
```

`read_csv2` is designed for the convention used in much of Europe, where `;` is the delimiter and `,` is the *decimal mark* (e.g. `14,99`).
It therefore treats the `.` in `14.99` as a thousands separator, so the price `14.99` becomes `1499` and the rating `4.2` becomes `42`.
Notice that `R` did not give an error; the only warning was an info message that is easy to ignore.
This is why you should always check your loaded data against the raw file!

:::

The file `data1.csv` contains student scores from two tests, with their average.

- [ ] How are missing scores recorded in the raw file, and what do they become when loaded into `R`? What else in the file was loaded as missing?
- [ ] Compute the mean of `score1`. Why do you get `NA`, and how can you fix this? (Hint: look at how `na.rm` was used in the notes.)
- [ ] Look at the row for Henry Zhao. Are his scores really `0`? What happens to the mean of `score1` and of `average` if he is excluded?

::: {.solution}

```{r}
students <- read_csv("data/part1/data1.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
students
```

Missing scores are recorded as empty fields (e.g. `85.0,,85.00`), which `read_csv` converts to `NA`.
The empty `notes` for Ivy Chen (`""`) has also been read as `NA`.

```{r}
students |>
    summarise(mean_score1 = mean(score1), mean_score1_narm = mean(score1, na.rm = TRUE))
```

Any calculation involving an `NA` gives `NA`, since `R` can't know what the missing value is.
Setting `na.rm = TRUE` removes the missing values before computing the mean.

```{r}
students |>
    filter(name != "Henry Zhao") |>
    summarise(mean_score1 = mean(score1, na.rm = TRUE), mean_average = mean(average))
```

Henry's notes say he was "Absent", so his scores of `0` really mean "did not take the test", and should arguably be missing (`NA`) rather than `0`.
Including him lowers the mean of `score1` from about 80 to about 71.
Whether that is right depends on the question: for "how well did students who sat the test do?" he should be excluded, but for "what marks were awarded?" a `0` might be correct.
This kind of problem can't be detected by `R`; you have to look at the data.

:::

The file `data2.txt` contains readings from air quality monitoring stations.

- [ ] Create a `tibble` containing only `station_id` and the particulate matter readings (the columns measured in µg/m³). Use a tidyselect helper rather than typing out the column names.

::: {.solution}

```{r}
air_quality <- read_tsv("data/part1/data2.txt", show_col_types = FALSE)

air_quality |>
    select(station_id, ends_with("_ug_m3"))
```

The two particulate columns both end in `_ug_m3`, so `ends_with` selects them without listing them by hand.

:::

- [ ] How many readings are there in the file, and from how many different neighbourhoods? (Hint: look at the "Other Summarise Functions" tip in the notes.)

::: {.solution}

```{r}
air_quality |>
    summarise(n_readings = n(), n_neighbourhoods = n_distinct(neighborhood))
```

`n()` counts the rows, while `n_distinct()` counts the number of unique values in a column.

:::

- [ ] Which readings have a `status` other than `OK`? What do you notice about their pollution readings and `sensor_uptime_pct`?
- [ ] Compute the mean `pm2_5_ug_m3` over all readings, and over only the readings with status `OK`. Which would you report, and why?

::: {.solution}

```{r}
air_quality |>
    filter(status != "OK") |>
    select(station_id, neighborhood, pm2_5_ug_m3, pm10_ug_m3, sensor_uptime_pct, status)
```

Station `AQ-012` has status `ERROR`, a low uptime, and no pollution readings at all (`NA`).
The two `MAINT` readings, both in Harbor, do have values, but a sensor under maintenance may not be reliable.

```{r}
air_quality |>
    summarise(mean_pm2_5 = mean(pm2_5_ug_m3, na.rm = TRUE))

air_quality |>
    filter(status == "OK") |>
    summarise(mean_pm2_5 = mean(pm2_5_ug_m3))
```

Removing the `ERROR` reading happens automatically with `na.rm = TRUE`, but the `MAINT` readings are only removed if we filter on `status`.
Reporting the mean over `OK` readings only is the safer choice, but whatever you choose, you should say which readings were excluded and why.

:::

### Task 2: `dplyr`

The `diamonds` dataset is included as a part of `ggplot2`.
If you have loaded `tidyverse` it should be already in your environment.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
diamonds
```

It contains information about `r nrow(diamonds)` diamonds.
Each row is a diamond, and each column contains information about that diamond such as:

- `price`: The price of the diamond in US dollars.
- `carat`: The weight of the diamond (1 carat = 0.2g).
- `cut`: Quality of the cut.
- `color`: The color of the diamond.
- `clarity`: A measure of how clear the diamond is.
- `depth`: Total depth percentage; $= \frac{z}{\frac{1}{2}(x + y)} \times 100$.
- `table`: Width of the top of the diamond relative to the widest point.
- `x`: Length of the diamond in mm.
- `y`: Width of the diamond in mm.
- `z`: Depth of the diamond in mm.

For the next few tasks you should use `dplyr` functions, using pipe syntax.
Try to format your code nicely so it is readable.


- [ ] Add a new column to the `tibble` called `volume` that contains the volume of the diamond ($x \times y \times z$).


::: {.solution}

```{r}
diamonds <- diamonds |> mutate(volume = x * y * z)
```
:::

- [ ] Create a `tibble` containing only the numeric columns of `diamonds`. (Hint: look at the tidyselect callout in the notes.)

::: {.solution}

```{r}
diamonds |> select(where(is.numeric))
```

`where(is.numeric)` selects every column for which `is.numeric` returns `TRUE`, dropping the factor columns `cut`, `color` and `clarity`.

:::

Now answer the following research questions.

- [ ] What is the average price of all the diamonds in the dataset?
- [ ] What is the volume of the 5 highest priced diamonds?
- [ ] What is the average, minimum and maximum price of diamonds for each cut?
- [ ] Ideal is the best cut, yet it has the lowest average price. Can you explain why? (Hint: compare the average `carat` of each cut.)
- [ ] For each cut, what is the average price-per-carat for diamonds with that cut?
- [ ] What are the most common combinations of cut and colour? (Hint: look up the `count` function)
- [ ] Create a `tibble` containing diamonds that are "unusually" large (having volume more than three standard deviations from the mean volume)?

::: {.solution}

```{r}
diamonds |>
    summarise(mean_price = mean(price))

diamonds |>
    arrange(desc(price)) |>
    select(price, volume) |>
    head(5)

diamonds |>
    group_by(cut) |>
    summarise(mean_price = mean(price), min_price = min(price), max_price = max(price)) |>
    arrange(desc(mean_price))

diamonds |>
    group_by(cut) |>
    summarise(mean_price = mean(price), mean_carat = mean(carat)) |>
    arrange(desc(mean_price))
```

Ideal diamonds are, on average, the smallest, and size has a much bigger effect on price than cut does.
So Ideal diamonds are cheaper on average not *because* of their cut, but because they tend to be smaller.
When two variables (here cut and carat) are related like this, comparing averages for one of them can be very misleading; this is called *confounding*.
The price-per-carat in the next question partly adjusts for size.

```{r}
diamonds |>
    mutate(price_per_carat = price / carat) |>
    group_by(cut) |>
    summarise(mean_price_per_carat = mean(price_per_carat)) |>
    arrange(desc(mean_price_per_carat))

diamonds |>
    count(cut, color, name = "n") |>
    arrange(desc(n)) |>
    head()

diamonds |>
    filter(volume > mean(volume) + 3 * sd(volume)) |>
    arrange(desc(volume))
```

:::

Before trusting these results, it is worth checking whether they make sense. Since all diamonds have the same density, heavier diamonds are larger, so `carat` and `volume` should be closely related.

- [ ] Look at the largest few diamonds in your answer. Given their `carat`, are their volumes plausible?
- [ ] Add a new column called `volume_per_carat` containing the ratio of `volume` to `carat`. Look at the diamonds with the smallest and largest values of this ratio. Does this suggest there any errors in the dataset?
- [ ] Create a new `tibble` called `diamonds_clean` that keeps only diamonds with `volume_per_carat` between 100 and 250. How many diamonds did you remove?
- [ ] Repeat the "unusually large" question using `diamonds_clean`. How many diamonds do you find now, and why has the number changed?

::: {.solution}

```{r}
diamonds <- diamonds |> mutate(volume_per_carat = volume / carat)

diamonds |>
    filter(volume_per_carat == 0) |>
    select(carat, x, y, z, volume, volume_per_carat)

diamonds |>
    filter(volume_per_carat > 0) |>
    arrange(volume_per_carat) |>
    select(carat, x, y, z, volume, volume_per_carat) |>
    head(10)

diamonds |>
    arrange(desc(volume_per_carat)) |>
    select(carat, x, y, z, volume, volume_per_carat) |>
    head(10)
```

Most diamonds have a `volume_per_carat` of around `r round(median(diamonds$volume_per_carat))`, but there are some clear errors:

- 20 diamonds have at least one dimension recorded as 0, giving a volume (and ratio) of 0.
- Three diamonds have `z` equal to their `carat` (e.g. `carat = 1.07`, `z = 1.07`), which looks like the wrong value was copied into the `z` column.
- Three diamonds have a `y` or `z` value of over 30mm, which looks like a typing error (e.g. `58.9` instead of `5.89`). These are the "largest" diamonds from the previous question!

The other diamonds with unusual ratios (e.g. around 90 or 320) are less clear-cut: they could be errors, or genuinely unusually-shaped diamonds. Choosing where to draw the line is a judgement call.

```{r}
diamonds_clean <- diamonds |>
    filter(volume_per_carat > 100, volume_per_carat < 250)
nrow(diamonds) - nrow(diamonds_clean)

diamonds_clean |>
    filter(volume > mean(volume) + 3 * sd(volume)) |>
    arrange(desc(volume))
```

We removed `r nrow(diamonds) - nrow(diamonds_clean)` diamonds, and now find *more* unusually large diamonds than before.
This is because the few enormous erroneous volumes inflated the standard deviation, raising the threshold for a diamond to count as "unusual".
The largest diamonds are now genuinely large (4--5 carats).
This shows how sensitive the mean and standard deviation are to a small number of bad values, and why you should always sanity-check your data.

:::

- [ ] **Extension:** Find the most expensive diamond of each cut.

::: {.solution}

```{r}
diamonds |>
    group_by(cut) |>
    filter(price == max(price)) |>
    ungroup() |>
    arrange(cut)
```

After `group_by(cut)`, `max(price)` is computed separately *within each cut*, so the `filter` keeps the most expensive diamond of each cut rather than the single most expensive diamond overall.
Unlike `summarise`, `filter` does not remove any grouping, so we use `ungroup()` afterwards.
If two diamonds of the same cut tied for the highest price, both would be kept.
Notice that the most expensive Good diamond has `z = 0`: it is one of the errors we found earlier! Its price may well be correct, but its dimensions are not.

:::


### Task 3: `tidyr`

The file `data/part3/assessment.csv` contains a messy student scores table.
It records the student's scores out of 100 across 8 possible assessments.
However, not all students take all assessments, and assessments the student has not taken are recorded as `NA`.

- [ ] Load the file and look at it. Recall the three rules of tidy data from the notes. Is this table tidy? If not, which rule(s) does it break?

::: {.solution}

```{r}
#| message: false
read_csv("data/part3/assessment.csv")
```

The table is not tidy.
Each observation is one student's score on one assessment, and the variables are the student, the semester, the assessment and the score.

- *Each variable is a column*: the semester and the assessment are variables, but their values (e.g. `Semester1`, `A1`) are stored in the column *names* rather than in columns of their own.
- *Each observation is a row*: each row contains up to 8 observations (one per assessment) rather than one.

Each cell does contain a single value, so the third rule is satisfied, for now!

:::

- [ ] Tidy the table: pivot into long format with one row per student and assessment, and drop missing scores.
- [ ] Compute each student's overall average, and the number of assessments they took. (Hint: look at the "Other Summarise Functions" tip in the notes.)

::: {.solution}

```{r}
#| message: false
student_data <- read_csv("data/part3/assessment.csv")

student_data_long <- student_data |>
    pivot_longer(
        cols = -student_id,
        names_to = "assessment",
        values_to = "score"
    ) |>
    drop_na(score)
student_means <- student_data_long |>
    group_by(student_id) |>
    summarise(mean_score = mean(score), n_assessments = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(mean_score))
student_means |> head()
```
:::

- [ ] Redo the pivot, this time using `starts_with` to choose the columns to pivot. Check you get the same result. Suppose a new column `student_name` were added to the file: which of the two approaches would still work, and why?

::: {.solution}

```{r}
student_data |>
    pivot_longer(
        cols = starts_with("Semester"),
        names_to = "assessment",
        values_to = "score"
    ) |>
    drop_na(score)
```

Both approaches give the same result here.
However, `-student_id` means "every column except `student_id`", so a new `student_name` column would be pivoted too, mixing names in with the scores (in fact `pivot_longer` would give an error, since it can't combine text and numbers in one column).
`starts_with("Semester")` only picks out the assessment columns, so it would keep working.
Choosing columns by what they *are*, rather than by what they are not, is usually more robust.

:::

One of the key principles of tidy data is that each cell should contain only one value.
Notice that in the new dataset, the column `assessment` contains *two* values: the Semester and the Assessment ID,
separated by an `_`.

- [ ] Use `separate_wider_delim` to split `assessment` into two columns, one with the assessment ID and one with the Semester.
- [ ] Create a wide table with one row per student, and two new columns containing the average score in Semester 1 and Semester 2.

::: {.solution}
```{r}
student_data_split <- student_data_long |>
    separate_wider_delim(assessment, delim = "_", names = c("semester", "assessment"))
student_data_split |> head(10)
student_data_wide <- student_data_split |>
    group_by(student_id, semester) |>
    summarise(mean_score = mean(score), .groups = "drop") |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = semester, values_from = mean_score)
student_data_wide
```
:::

- [ ] Add a column `improvement` to the wide table showing how much each student's average score changed from Semester 1 to Semester 2. Which students improved the most, and which declined the most?

::: {.solution}
```{r}
student_improvement <- student_data_wide |>
    mutate(improvement = Semester2 - Semester1)

student_improvement |>
    arrange(desc(improvement)) |>
    head()

student_improvement |>
    arrange(improvement) |>
    head()
```

Having one column per semester makes this a simple `mutate`; in the long format we would first have to match up each student's two semester averages.
:::

- [ ] **Extension:** We tidied this dataset in two steps: `pivot_longer` followed by `separate_wider_delim`. Can you do both in a single call to `pivot_longer`? (Hint: look at the `names_sep` argument in `?pivot_longer`.)

::: {.solution}
```{r}
student_data_onestep <- student_data |>
    pivot_longer(
        cols = starts_with("Semester"),
        names_to = c("semester", "assessment"),
        names_sep = "_",
        values_to = "score"
    ) |>
    drop_na(score)
student_data_onestep |> head(10)

identical(student_data_onestep, student_data_split)
```

Giving `names_to` two names and setting `names_sep = "_"` tells `pivot_longer` to split each column name at the `_` as it pivots, so the result is identical to the two-step version.
:::
